title: BTOM — the £330M/year quiet Brexit tax
hook: Three years after leaving the single market, the UK started actually checking EU food imports. The running cost of those checks is now roughly £330 million a year — paid by importers and passed to consumers.
lede: The Border Target Operating Model (BTOM), phased in during 2024, finally implemented SPS and customs checks on EU-origin goods coming into Great Britain — checks that had been waived since Brexit took effect in 2021. Government estimated direct costs at £330m/year. The OBR estimated long-run trade intensity with the EU will be around 15% lower than it would have been without Brexit.

narrative_md:
**Three years after leaving the single market, the UK started actually checking EU food imports. The running cost of those checks is now roughly £330 million a year — paid by importers and passed to consumers.**

The Border Target Operating Model (BTOM), phased in during 2024, finally implemented SPS and customs checks on EU-origin goods coming into Great Britain — checks that had been waived since Brexit took effect in 2021. Government estimated direct costs at £330m/year. The OBR estimated long-run trade intensity with the EU will be around 15% lower than it would have been without Brexit.

**The history.** On leaving the EU single market on 1 January 2021, the UK should immediately have started customs and SPS (Sanitary and Phytosanitary) checks on EU imports. It did not. The Johnson, Truss and Sunak governments postponed the checks six times — in 2021, April 2022, July 2022, April 2023, October 2023 and January 2024 — citing pandemic disruption, supply-chain risk, and inflation pressures. The EU, by contrast, implemented full checks on UK exports from day one, imposing significant friction on UK food and drink exporters.

**BTOM delivery.** The current model was published in the Sunak government's August 2023 BTOM document. Phase 1 (31 January 2024): medium-risk EU animal products and plants require Export Health Certificates. Phase 2 (30 April 2024): physical documentary and identity checks begin at Border Control Posts — Sevington (near Ashford, Kent) is the flagship, displacing Dover itself. Phase 3 (31 October 2024): full risk-based sampling and laboratory testing for high-risk commodities. A simplified regime applies to Northern Ireland movements under the Windsor Framework 'green lane'.

**The costs.** The Government's impact assessment put direct recurring costs at £330m/year — certificates, laboratory testing, delays, paperwork, BCP operating costs. The Food and Drink Federation put the SME-borne cost higher, around £1bn of trade intensity reduction for the smaller end of the industry. The Cold Chain Federation reported load consolidations — multiple SMEs being forced to ship through a single freight forwarder because individual consignments were no longer commercially viable with the new paperwork.

**The trade-intensity finding.** The OBR in March 2024 confirmed its long-run assumption: UK-EU trade in goods and services will be around 15% lower than it would have been without Brexit, with a 4-percentage-point contribution attributable to BTOM-style non-tariff barriers. Rebuild of lost EU food-chain connections is slow: the Government's target to rejoin EU Veterinary Agreement (Starmer's 'reset' language from 2024-25) would substantially reduce BTOM costs but remains in negotiation.

**Who pays.** Economic incidence falls primarily on UK consumers (through retail food prices — BRC estimates +1-2% on some fresh categories), UK SMEs importing EU perishables, and EU exporters with UK market concentration (Dutch horticulture, Irish dairy, Spanish citrus). The Dover Strait lanes lost some throughput to Sevington inland; Dutch and Belgian ports quietly expanded alternative routings into UK deep-sea ports.

**The Sevington question.** The £95m BCP at Sevington has operated below its design throughput since April 2024 — traders routed around it, consolidated loads, or accepted delays. Kent County Council has complained about traffic impact; the Freight Transport Association disputes operational utility. Whether Sevington becomes the standing architecture of UK-EU goods trade, or a transitional facility dismantled under a future Veterinary Agreement, will be decided in the 2025-27 EU reset negotiations. The £330m/year is a standing charge, and will compound through price signals, for however long friction remains.
